issue: Source: 'if the exercise of the power of internal taxation by the Union should be discovered on experiment to be really inconvenient, the federal government may then forbear the use of it'. Candidate drops 'by the Union' (flagged 'the Union' loss): 'the federal government need not keep using internal taxation if experience shows it to be really inconvenient'. Restores the Union as the exerciser of the power; keeps 'federal government' as the one that may forbear.
replacement: Various speakers and writers on the side of the Constitution have rightly pointed out that if the exercise of the power of internal taxation by the Union should prove on experiment to be really inconvenient, the federal government may then give up the use of it and go back to requisitions, the formal requests to the States for money. To this, opponents have triumphantly replied: why not leave out that ambiguous power in the first place and depend on the other resource? Two solid answers can be given. First, if the power turns out to be convenient, it will be preferable because it will be more effective, and no theory can prove, nor anything but experiment, that it cannot be used to advantage. Indeed the opposite seems most probable. Second, simply having such a power in the Constitution will give requisitions a strong influence. When the States know that the Union can act without their help, they will have a powerful motive to make an effort themselves.

issue: Source reads 'those intrusted with it should be kept in independence on the people, by a short duration of their appointments' (almost certainly a misprint for 'dependence'). Candidate silently repairs it: 'be kept dependent on the people'. Brief: a misprint stays as the source reads and is listed as an open issue. Replacement follows the source word 'independence'.
replacement: One very important difficulty the Convention met must have been the task of combining the necessary stability and energy in government with unfailing attention to liberty and to the republican form. If they had not substantially accomplished this part of their task, they would have fulfilled very imperfectly the object of their appointment and the expectation of the public. Yet no one who does not wish to betray his ignorance of the subject will deny that it could not easily be accomplished. Energy in government is essential to security against external and internal danger, and to the prompt and beneficial execution of the laws, both of which enter into the very definition of good government. Stability in government is essential to national character and the advantages that go with it, and also to that repose and confidence in the minds of the people which are among the chief blessings of civil society. A changeable and irregular legislation is no more an evil in itself than it is odious to the people. It may be said with assurance that the people of this country, enlightened as they are about the nature of good government and concerned as the great body of them are in its effects, will never be satisfied until some remedy is applied to the vicissitudes and uncertainties that mark the State administrations. But when we compare these valuable ingredients with the vital principles of liberty, we see at once how hard it is to mix them in their due proportions. The spirit of republican liberty seems to demand, on one side, not only that all power be derived from the people but that those entrusted with it be kept in independence on the people by the short duration of their appointments. It seems to demand also that even during this short period the trust be placed not in a few hands but in a number of them. Stability, on the contrary, requires that the hands in which power is lodged remain the same for a length of time. Frequent elections will bring a frequent change of men, and a frequent change of men will bring a frequent change of measures. Energy in government, meanwhile, requires not only a certain duration of power but that it be exercised by a single hand.

issue: Source 'sacrificing private opinions and partial interests to the public good'. Candidate keeps archaic 'partial interests', which a modern reader will take as 'incomplete' (STYLE-NOTE: partial -> biased/partisan by context; here the sense is particular/narrow interests). Use 'particular interests'.
replacement: In an earlier paper we had occasion to notice the repeated and unsuccessful attempts made in the United Netherlands to reform the baneful and notorious vices of their constitution. The history of almost all the great councils and consultations held among mankind to reconcile their discordant opinions, calm their mutual jealousies and adjust their respective interests is a history of factions, contentions and disappointments. It may be ranked among the darkest and most degraded pictures that show the infirmities and depravities of the human character. If a few scattered instances present a brighter aspect, they serve only as exceptions that remind us of the general truth, and by their luster they deepen the gloom of the opposite prospect with which they are contrasted. When we consider the causes of these exceptions and apply them to the particular instance before us, we are necessarily led to two important conclusions. The first is that the Convention must have enjoyed, to a very singular degree, freedom from the pestilential influence of party animosities, the disease most common to deliberative bodies and most likely to contaminate their proceedings. The second conclusion is that all the deputations that made up the Convention were either satisfactorily accommodated by the final act or were brought to agree to it by a deep conviction of the necessity of sacrificing private opinions and particular interests to the public good, and by despair of seeing this necessity lessened by delay or by new experiments.

issue: Source: the Senate 'which is alternately a member both of the legislative and executive departments'. Candidate: 'which is at once a member of both'. 'Alternately' (taking turns) became 'at once' (simultaneously), changing Madison's claim. Restore 'alternately'.
replacement: America at this moment is such a patient in such a situation. She has been aware of her malady. She has obtained regular and unanimous advice from men of her own careful choosing. And others warn her against following this advice, on pain of the most fatal consequences. Do the advisers deny that her danger is real? No. Do they deny the need of some speedy and powerful remedy? No. Are they agreed, are even any two of them agreed, in their objections to the proposed remedy or in the proper one to put in its place? Let them speak for themselves. This one tells us that the proposed Constitution ought to be rejected because it is not a confederation of the States but a government over individuals. Another admits that it ought to be a government over individuals to a certain extent, but by no means to the extent proposed. A third does not object to a government over individuals, or to the extent proposed, but to the lack of a bill of rights. A fourth agrees that a bill of rights is absolutely necessary, but argues that it ought to declare, not the personal rights of individuals, but the rights reserved to the States in their political capacity. A fifth is of the opinion that a bill of rights of any sort would be superfluous and out of place, and that the plan would be beyond objection but for the fatal power of regulating the times and places of election. An objector in a large State cries out loudly against the unreasonable equality of representation in the Senate. An objector in a small State is equally loud against the dangerous inequality in the House of Representatives. From one quarter we are alarmed at the amazing expense, owing to the number of persons who are to run the new government. From another quarter, and sometimes from the same quarter on another occasion, the cry is that Congress will be only a shadow of a representation, and that the government would be far less objectionable if the number and the expense were doubled. A patriot in a State that does not import or export finds insuperable objections to the power of direct taxation. The patriotic adversary in a State with great exports and imports is no less dissatisfied that the whole burden of taxes may be thrown on consumption. This politician discovers in the Constitution a direct and irresistible tendency to monarchy; that one is equally sure it will end in aristocracy. Another is puzzled to say which of these shapes it will finally take, but sees clearly that it must be one or the other. And a fourth is not lacking who, with no less confidence, affirms that the Constitution is so far from leaning toward either of these dangers that the weight on that side will not be enough to keep it upright and firm against its opposite tendencies. With another class of adversaries to the Constitution the language is that the legislative, executive and judiciary departments are intermixed in such a way as to contradict all ideas of regular government and all the precautions needed in favor of liberty. While this objection circulates in vague and general terms, few lend it their support. Let each one come forward with his own explanation, and scarcely any two are exactly agreed on the subject. In the eyes of one, the vicious part of the organization is the joining of the Senate with the President in the responsible function of appointing to offices, instead of vesting this executive power in the Executive alone. To another, the exclusion of the House of Representatives is equally offensive, since its numbers alone could be a proper security against corruption and bias in exercising such a power. For another, letting the President have any share in a power that must always be a dangerous engine in the hands of the chief executive is an unpardonable violation of the maxims of republican jealousy. According to some, no part of the arrangement is more inadmissible than trying impeachments before the Senate, which is alternately a member of both the legislative and executive departments, when this power so obviously belonged to the judiciary department. "We concur fully," others reply, "in the objection to this part of the plan, but we can never agree that a reference of impeachments to the judiciary authority would be an amendment of the error. Our principal dislike to the organization arises from the extensive powers already lodged in that department." Even among the zealous supporters of a council of state, the most irreconcilable disagreement is found over how it ought to be constituted. One gentleman demands that the council consist of a small number, to be appointed by the most numerous branch of the legislature. Another would prefer a larger number, and regards it as a fundamental condition that the appointment be made by the President himself.

issue: Source: 'So far the national countenance of the government on this side seems to be disfigured by a few federal features.' Candidate: 'To that extent a few federal features disfigure the national countenance'. The hedge 'seems to be' is dropped, so Madison's softened claim becomes flat assertion. Restore the qualifier.
replacement: As it concerns the OPERATION OF THE GOVERNMENT, the difference between a federal and a national government is supposed to be this. In a federal government the powers act on the political bodies that make up the Confederacy, in their political capacities. In a national government they act on the individual citizens who make up the nation, in their individual capacities. Tested by this criterion, the Constitution falls under the NATIONAL character, not the FEDERAL, though perhaps not so completely as has been understood. In several cases, and especially in trying controversies to which States may be parties, the States must be regarded and proceeded against only in their collective and political capacities. To that extent the national countenance of the government on this side seems to be disfigured by a few federal features. But this blemish is perhaps unavoidable in any plan. And because the government acts on the people in their individual capacities in its ordinary and most essential proceedings, we may on the whole call it, in this relation, a NATIONAL government.

issue: Source is one question: 'Is it an unreasonable conjecture, that the errors ... are such as have resulted rather from ... antecedent experience ... than from a want of accuracy or care; and, consequently such as will not be ascertained until an actual trial shall have pointed them out?' Candidate splits the last clause into a second question 'is it not so that these errors will not be found...', which turns the conjecture into a leading assertion. Meaning is close; optional restoration to one question.
replacement: Is it an unreasonable conjecture that whatever errors the plan of the Convention contains are such as have resulted from lack of earlier experience in this complicated and difficult subject, rather than from any lack of accuracy or care in investigating it, and consequently are such as will not be found until an actual trial has pointed them out? Many considerations of a general nature make this conjecture probable, and so does the particular case of the Articles of Confederation. Notice that when these articles were submitted to the individual States for ratification, they produced numerous objections and proposed amendments. Not one of them alludes to the great and radical error that actual trial has since uncovered. If we except the observations that New Jersey was led to make by her local situation rather than by any special foresight, it may be doubted whether a single suggestion was weighty enough to justify revising the system. There is nevertheless abundant reason to suppose that, trivial as these objections were, some States would have clung to them with very dangerous inflexibility, had their zeal for their opinions and supposed interests not been stifled by the more powerful feeling of self-preservation. We may remember that one State persisted for several years in refusing her agreement, although the enemy remained the whole time at our gates, or rather in the very bowels of our country. In the end she was brought around by no weaker motive than the fear of being blamed for prolonging the public calamities and endangering the outcome of the contest. Every fair-minded reader will draw the proper reflections from these important facts.
